_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
tosafot:a1.1: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Everyone concedes, etc. [Tosafot reads “Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef” where the Davidson English has “Rabbi Yitzḥak, son of Rabbi Yosei.”] This is the approach according to Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef: Rabbi Meir’s reason is not that we attend to the first expression. Had one said “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” even Rabbi Meir would concede that both take effect. Rabbi Meir disagrees only about “the substitute of the burnt offering, the substitute of the peace offering,” as it explains: since he should have said “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” etc. And Rabbi Yosei holds [that the man reasoned]: If I say “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” it will be consecrated but not sacrificed, that is, I will not be able to sacrifice it, since half of it will be the substitute of a burnt offering and half of it the substitute of a peace offering; let me say “the substitute of the burnt offering, the substitute of the peace offering,” and it will be sacrificed. Therefore [the sanctity] takes effect for both, since he intended both.
rashi:a3.1: Gemara. We read: “The substitute of the burnt offering, the substitute of the peace offering”; we do not read “and the substitute of the peace offering.”
gershom:a2.1: Rather, by right: he should have said “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” and that would have sufficed. But since he said “the substitute of the burnt offering, the substitute of the peace offering,” we therefore examine him, etc.
rashi:a4.1:
And Rabbi Yosei holds: if I say “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” etc.: Rabbi Yosei would tell you that this man reasoned: If I use the expression “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” it will be consecrated but not sacrificed. And he erred in this, thinking: I will say “substitute” over each one, and it will be fully consecrated, to be sacrificed. Therefore, even though he spoke in this way, he intended both, and it is like one who says: This shall not take effect unless that takes effect.
A version from the Land of Israel [lashon Yerushalmi]: Rabbi Meir holds that this man, who said “the substitute of the burnt offering and the substitute of the peace offering,” is one who broke off [his words], reasoning, “if I do not say…,” etc.; he is one who retracted. And the baraita is taught calmly [as a support, not as a challenge], since this is their dispute. Rabbi Yosei is the same as the Rabbis, for certainly when the Rabbis too say that both take effect, they say so only where he intended this from the outset; where he reconsidered, everyone agrees that his later words are nothing, for he certainly cannot reconsider.
gershom:a1.1: Another version: the second also takes effect. And Rabbi Yosei holds: had he said “the substitute of the burnt offering and the peace offering,” and not also said “substitute” over the peace offering, I would have said that it is consecrated as the substitute of a peace offering [and is not sacrificed; it teaches us that this is why he also said “the substitute of the peace offering”] (and its money does not go to a substitute peace offering, since he did not also say “substitute” over the peace offering), so that it would also be sacrificed as a peace offering. [The bracketed and parenthetical words are the printed text’s emendation and its deleted reading.] Another version explains the reasons of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei as in the first version.
gershom:a3.1: And it is taught [in a baraita]: [it is cited as] a support.
tosafot:a5.1:
In brief: One who says “this animal, half of it the substitute of a burnt offering and half of it the substitute of a peace offering”: it is sacrificed entirely as a burnt offering, the statement of Rabbi Meir. Tosafot asks: according to Rabbi Yitzḥak son of Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Meir’s reason is “since he should have said…,” not that we attend to the first expression; that reasoning does not apply here, so why is it sacrificed as a burnt offering? The same question arises in the mishna, “it is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering,” where Rabbi Meir says it is the offspring of a peace offering. Tosafot answers: that reasoning is needed only for “the substitute of the burnt offering, the substitute of the peace offering,” which sounds as though he contradicts his own words; without it one would say he intended both, since a person does not normally contradict himself so plainly. In the mishna there are two bodies, and here he specifies the halves, so there is no contradiction and he may well have intended both; but as soon as he said “half of it the substitute of a burnt offering,” it took effect on all of it (and in the mishna, as soon as he said “it is a peace offering,” the sanctity took effect on the offspring). Tosafot leaves for further study Zevaḥim 30b, on “an olive-bulk and an olive-bulk.”
A second question: how can Rabbi Meir say it is all sacrificed as a burnt offering, when in the first chapter (above, 11b) he holds like Rabbi Yehuda that one who says “the leg of this animal is a burnt offering” has not made all of it a burnt offering? And if Rabbi Yehuda concedes for a limb on which life depends, and half is such a limb, it was said there (11a) that this applies to initial consecration but not to substitution, since one does not substitute limbs for peace offerings. Tosafot answers that Rabbi Meir agrees with Rabbi Yehuda on one point and disagrees on another: he agrees that “its leg is a burnt offering” does not make all of it a burnt offering, but he holds with Rabbi Yosei, who compares substitution to initial consecration (10a: “Just as with consecrated animals, one who says ‘its leg is a burnt offering’ makes all of it a burnt offering, so too ‘its leg in place of this’ makes all of it a substitute”), that substitution on a limb on which life depends takes effect on all of it. Rabbi Yehuda holds substitution never takes effect on a limb, even one on which life depends, for the reasons given in the first chapter (11a): either he derives “animal for animal,” or he compares substitution to the tithe, which is an individual’s offering. Alternatively, even Rabbi Yehuda concedes for “half of it,” since half differs from a limb on which life depends. That distinction is needed for Rabbi Yosei too, who says “and not whole ones for them” yet concedes that one may substitute for a half, as Tosafot explains below. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a4.1: “This is the substitute of the burnt offering,” etc.: Rabbi Yosei is the same as the Sages. Since he said “his statement stands,” he too holds that it is sold and he brings [offerings with its money], etc. Yes, certainly he holds like the Rabbis. And this teaches us who the Sages are: Rabbi Yosei.
gershom:a5.1: The Sages taught: One who says “this animal, half of it the substitute of a burnt offering,” etc. The explanation is as in the baraita above, that the Sages are Rabbi Yosei, except that he abbreviates the baraita.
rashi:a7.1: Half of the animal a burnt offering and half of it a sin offering, it is sacrificed as a burnt offering: since he holds that we attend to the first expression, and since half of it was consecrated with the sanctity of a burnt offering, all of it is consecrated. And even though, with regard to one who says “the leg of this animal is a burnt offering,” Rabbi Meir did not say that the sanctity takes effect on all of it, as taught in our chapter (18a), even so he concedes in the case of half, as we say there: everyone agrees about something on which life depends.
gershom:a6.1: It is sacrificed entirely as a burnt offering: since he said “half of it a burnt offering,” the sanctity took hold of all of it. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir, for here we certainly say that we attend to the first expression. And Rabbi Yosei says it must die, since the sanctity of both takes effect on it, and since he is not obligated to bring a sin offering it is like a sin offering whose owner has achieved atonement [so the printed correction; the deleted reading is “whose owner died”], for this one likewise is left over without his needing it, since he is not obligated to bring a sin offering. Therefore it must die.
rashi:a8.1: It must die: since a person is bound even by the conclusion of his statement, and he is not obligated to bring a sin offering; therefore it must die.
tosafot:a8.1: Rabbi Yosei says: It must die. Rashi explains that a person is bound even by the conclusion of his statement, and he is not obligated to bring a sin offering; therefore it must die. This is difficult: how does the sanctity of a sin offering take effect on it at all? It says in Nedarim (6a) that even if one said of an animal “this is a sin offering,” if he is not obligated to bring a sin offering he has said nothing. Therefore the Ri explains that here the case is where he said “and half of it the substitute of a sin offering.” And so we read in the Tosefta [chapter 3]: “This animal, half of it in place of a burnt offering and half of it in place of a sin offering: it is sacrificed as a burnt offering. Rabbi Yosei says: It must die.” Rabbi Yosei’s reason is that both take effect, and since the substitute of a sin offering is on it, it goes to death.
rashi:a8.2: And they agree about one who says “half of it a sin offering” first, and then “half of it a burnt offering,” that it must die.
gershom:a7.1: And they agree about one who says first “half of it a sin offering” and afterward “half of it a burnt offering,” that it must die: for even according to Rabbi Meir, who says we attend to the first expression, since he first said “half of it a sin offering,” and he is not obligated to bring a sin offering, it is like a sin offering whose owner has achieved atonement, and it must die.
rashi:a9.1: They agree: who [is conceding]? Rabbi Meir. For perforce this is the meaning: even Rabbi Meir, who said in the first clause that it is sacrificed, [agrees that] here it must die. And this is obvious, since Rabbi Meir holds that we attend to the first expression, and since he said “half of it a sin offering” first, all the more so it must die, since he is not obligated to bring a sin offering.
rashi:a10.1: Mixed: two sanctities were mixed in it, and even though both of them take effect on it, it is sacrificed, since something fit to be sacrificed is mixed into it. [The baraita] teaches us [that this is not his reason].
gershom:a8.1: Lest you say this is the reason of Rabbi Meir, who says it is sacrificed as a burnt offering: that he holds a mixed sin offering is sacrificed, when he said “half of it a burnt offering and half of it a sin offering,” and even when he said, etc.
gershom:a9.1: It is consecrated but not sacrificed; it is sold, and he brings a burnt offering with the money of half of it and a peace offering with the money of half of it; and it renders [another animal] a substitute: since it is a male, which is fit for a burnt offering, [it has] inherent sanctity.
gershom:a10.1: It renders a substitute, and its substitute is like it: it is sold, and with the money of half of it he brings the substitute of a burnt offering, and with the money of half of it the substitute of a peace offering. Whose view is it? Rabbi Yosei’s, who says “his statement stands.”
gershom:a11.1: Obvious: that it is certainly Rabbi Yosei’s.
rashi:a14.1: It was necessary for its substitute: to teach us that it is like it and is not sacrificed; rather, it is sold after it becomes blemished, and he brings a burnt offering with the money of half of it and a peace offering with the money of half of it. Lest you say: granted that it itself is not sacrificed, etc.
tosafot:a14.1: Lest you say: granted that it itself is not sacrificed, its substitute is sacrificed. And if you ask: how could one think so, treating the substitute as weightier than the animal on whose account it comes? One may answer: lest you say that he did not intend the substitute to be half a burnt offering and half a peace offering, but rather that it be entirely a substitute, either in place of the half that is a burnt offering or in place of the half that is a peace offering, and so it would be sacrificed. And even though in the first chapter (above, 10a) Rabbi Yosei says that one does not substitute a whole animal for limbs, as we learned, “and not whole ones for them,” he concedes for half: if one said “this non-sacred animal is in place of half of that one,” it takes effect. This is what I explained above, that one must distinguish between half and other limbs. So, lest you say that its substitute is sacrificed even though it itself is not, it teaches us that it is not sacrificed, since it comes from the force of deferred sanctity.
gershom:a12.1: Lest you say its substitute is sacrificed: since over the substitute he mentioned neither a burnt offering nor a peace offering, but said only “this is the substitute of that.”
gershom:a13.1: It teaches us that it is not sacrificed: for what is different about it, that it is not sacrificed? Because it has a sanctity deferred from sacrifice, since it has two names. The substitute too comes from the force of deferred sanctity and is not sacrificed.
rashi:a15.1: And it is not sacrificed: since at the outset, when he consecrated half of it, it was not fit to be sacrificed, as he did not consecrate [the other] half of it. And since that was not his, the sanctity did not spread through all of it at that time, for a person cannot consecrate something that is not his.
gershom:a14.1: [He consecrated half of it: his share, and then acquired the other half from his fellow and consecrated it: it is consecrated but not sacrificed, because at the time he consecrated his share not all of it was his, and inherent sanctity did not take hold of it.]
gershom:a15.1: And it renders a substitute: for it is fit as an offering that is accepted. And its substitute is like it: it is sold and he brings [offerings] with its money, etc.
rashi:b1.1: Sanctity that inheres in value causes deferral: one who consecrates an animal for its value at a time when it is not fit for its body [to be offered], as here, where when he consecrated half of it, it was consecrated only for its value, and it is deferred from the altar forever. One might have thought that deferral takes effect only on something consecrated for the altar and then rejected.
tosafot:b1.1:
In brief: Some texts read “Conclude from it: sanctity that inheres in value causes deferral,” and some explain this as deferring the substitute, which is not sacrificed, as it says “and its substitute is like it.” Tosafot rejects this from the last chapter of Keritot (27b), on a rich man who became impure in the Temple, set aside a bird pair instead of his ewe, and became poor: since it was deferred, it stays deferred; and there too it says “conclude three things… sanctity that inheres in value causes deferral,” yet birds have no substitution. Rather, it means there is deferral even with value, that is, even with something that has only sanctity of value. If you ask that this still does not fit there, since birds have no redemption (Shekalim 4:8) and so no sanctity of value, the answer is that there it means deferral even of something without inherent sanctity, and the same holds even without sanctity of value.
Q: What does Rabbi Yoḥanan teach us, if all three are already concluded in Pesaḥim (98a), about one who sets aside a female for his Paschal offering? A: Tanna’im dispute whether living animals are deferred, and he teaches that he holds they are.
Q: Why say both “there is deferral with value” and “deferral at the outset is deferral,” if deferral at the outset is the case of sanctity of value? A: Deferral at the outset is found with inherent sanctity too: an apostate who ate forbidden fat and set aside an offering for it and recanted, or Zevaḥim (78a), blood that fell into water, where Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yoḥanan says each drop is nullified as it falls.
Q: Then why does Rabbi Yoḥanan himself (Zevaḥim 12b; Sanhedrin 47a) give the case as “ate fat, set aside an offering, became an apostate and recanted,” rather than the bolder “ate fat, became an apostate and set aside an offering”? A: Because of the parallel case there of one who became insane and recovered, where he could not say “became insane and set aside an offering,” since an insane person’s setting aside is nothing.
Q: How can Rabbi Yoḥanan hold that deferral at the outset is deferral, when in Yoma (64a) the view that living animals are not deferred is derived from an animal lacking time, and the other side answers that one was never fit, implying deferral only where it was once fit? A: There is another approach there, deriving it from “they shall not be accepted, for their blemish is in them,” not from lacking time; so he can hold that deferral at the outset is deferral, and the remark about lacking time came before the verse was known.
Q: In Keritot (27b–28a), Rabbi Oshaya’s bird pair yields the same three conclusions and is challenged from Rabbi Shimon (a female set aside for a Paschal offering gave birth to a male: it itself is sacrificed as a Paschal offering). Why not challenge Rabbi Yoḥanan as well? Why not support Rabbi Oshaya from the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Shimon (it grazes until blemished, is sold, and a Paschal offering is brought with its money)? And why not challenge from Rabbi Eliezer in our mishna above (18b), that the male born of a female set aside for a burnt offering is itself sacrificed? A: The questioner held that Rabbi Shimon follows his own view (19b, a female set aside for a guilt offering), that what is not fit for its own body does not receive inherent sanctity, against Rav Yehuda citing Rav, “since sanctity of value descends on it, inherent sanctity descends too.” So he challenged the bird pair, which has no inherent sanctity; he could not support it from the Rabbis, who disagree only where that reasoning applies, while birds have no redemption and no sanctity of value, so there even the Rabbis concede. That is also why he did not challenge Rabbi Yoḥanan, whose case fits “since sanctity of value descends…”; and he cited Rabbi Shimon’s baraita rather than Rabbi Eliezer’s mishna because Rabbi Shimon’s reason was more plausibly tied to his own view on 19b. The answer there is that it depends not on “since it descends” but on whether living animals are deferred: we follow the Rabbis, and Rabbi Shimon holds that living animals are not deferred. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b2.1: And conclude from it that sanctity that inheres in value causes deferral: for the animal has sanctity of value, and it defers it from sacrifice. And conclude from it about deferral at the outset: such as this one, which was deferred from the outset, at the time he consecrated his share, when it was not fit for sacrifice, is a deferral. Even though it was never fit for sacrifice, and even though it was so from the moment he consecrated it, it is a deferral. For it might enter your mind to say: what was fit and was deferred does not become fit again, but deferral at the outset is not a full deferral. It teaches us that the deferral is a deferral.
rashi:b2.1: Living animals are deferred: and even though they become fit again, they are deferred forever because of the first deferral.
gershom:b1.1: Conclude from it that living animals, which have no blemish, are deferred from sacrifice.
rashi:b2.2: Deferral at the outset: such as this one, which was deferred from the start of its consecration, is a deferral. And it is a dispute, for there is one who says (Sukka 33a): what was fit and was deferred does not become fit again, but deferral at the outset is not deferral.
rashi:b3.1: Half of it a burnt offering and half of it a tithe, everyone agrees it is sacrificed as a burnt offering: even if he intended this from the outset, since the latter word counts for nothing, for the tithe is not consecrated in this way, only by way of counting, when it is the tenth. The same is true if he said “half of it a burnt offering and half of it a substitute”: the substitution does not take effect alongside the burnt offering, since no animal is standing by it for him to substitute with.
tosafot:b3.1: Abaye said: Everyone concedes that if one said “half of it a burnt offering and half of it a tithe,” everyone agrees it is sacrificed as a burnt offering. Rashi explains: even if he intended this from the outset, since the latter word counts for nothing, as the tithe is not consecrated in this way but only by way of counting, when it is the tenth; and the same is true if he said “half of it a burnt offering and half of it a substitute,” the substitution does not take effect alongside the burnt offering, since no animal stands by it for him to substitute with; but with “half of it a tithe and half of it a substitute,” the two are alike, which takes effect? [End of Rashi’s words.] This is difficult: even if all of it were tithe, his words would be nothing. Furthermore, what is “or perhaps it is sacrificed as a tithe”? It is neither sacrificed nor consecrated except by counting. The Ri therefore explains that the case is one passing his flock under the rod, who said: When the tenth comes out of the pen, let half of it be a burnt offering and half of it a tithe. Everyone agrees it is sacrificed as a burnt offering, since the sanctity of speech by which he consecrated it as a burnt offering is stronger than the sanctity of the tithe, which can take effect only through counting the tenth and passing under the rod. Only with a burnt offering and a peace offering does [Rabbi Yosei; the printed text has “Rabbi Shimon” in parentheses] disagree and say that both take effect, since the sanctity of one is not so much stronger than the other; but with a burnt offering and a tithe, where the sanctity of the burnt offering is far stronger than that of the tithe, everyone agrees that his intent is for the burnt offering. And if you ask: why not say “the words of the master and the words of the student, whose words does one heed?”, as we said above at the start of the chapter about a firstborn, so that the tithe should take effect and not the burnt offering? One may answer that there he said of the firstborn, “when most of it emerges, let it be a burnt offering,” whereas here the case is that he said, “when a minority of it emerges, let it be a burnt offering and a tithe,” and the sanctity of the tithe does not take effect on it until most of it emerges.
gershom:b3.1: Everyone agrees it is a burnt offering: even according to Rabbi Yosei, since the half that is a tithe is not consecrated, for the tithe is consecrated only at the time it goes out from under the rod as the tenth.
rashi:b4.1: But half of it a tithe and half of it a substitute [Rashi gives the two in this order]: the two of them are alike; which one takes effect? Substitution applies to all [offerings].
gershom:b4.1: But where he said “half of it a substitute and half of it a tithe”: where he did not speak properly about either substitution or tithe, since a person does not say “this is a substitute” [plainly] unless he says “a substitute [in place of] this,” and likewise a person cannot say “this is a tithe” except at the time it goes out of the pen.
gershom:b5.1: And where he said it plainly, like this, “half of it a substitute and half of it a tithe,” what is it? As which is it sacrificed? It is sacrificed as a substitute, since it applies, etc.
gershom:b6.1: For it consecrates before it and after it: as we learned, if he called the ninth the tenth, etc., all three are consecrated.
gershom:b7.1: He reconsidered [the printed edition notes that Rabbeinu Gershom’s text had here “It is obvious…”, and “Rav Pappa said: It is necessary only…”, as above at the end of 25b]: it is obvious, since we attend to the first expression.
gershom:b8.1: It is necessary only: [where he reconsidered] even though within the time required for speaking, the time of a greeting [of] a master by a student. Lest you say it is like continuous speech, and that he paused and reconsidered because he was considering what he had meant to say, so as to join [the peace offering] with the burnt offering, so that his statement would stand and it would be the substitute of a burnt offering and a peace offering. It teaches us that it is not so.
rashi:b6.1: Mishna. “In place of this,” “the substitute of this,” “the exchange for this”: these are expressions of substitution.
rashi:b6.2: Desacralized: this is an expression of desacralization, and he has said nothing, for an unblemished consecrated animal does not go out to non-sacred status.
gershom:b9.1: One who said about an animal “this is in place of this,” or “let this be the substitute of this,” or “this is the exchange for this”: this is an expression of substitution, for substitution and exchange are written explicitly: “He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it” [Leviticus 27:10]. But if he said “let this be desacralized onto this,” that is not an expression of substitution, and he does not receive lashes.
rashi:b7.1: To conduct an appraisal for it: so that the non-sacred animal is worth as much as the consecrated animal he is desacralizing onto it, and the Temple treasury is not defrauded.
gershom:b10.1: And if the consecrated animal was blemished, and he said “this is desacralized onto this.”
gershom:b11.1: It goes out to non-sacred status, and this one enters in its place, for “this is desacralized onto this” means: let this one go out and that one enter. Certainly when the consecrated animal is unblemished and fit for sacrifice and he said “this is desacralized onto this,” his words are nothing and the consecrated animal does not go out to non-sacred status; but when it is blemished, it goes out to non-sacred status and this one enters in its place.
gershom:b12.1: And he must conduct an appraisal: for the consecrated animal, so that the one that enters in its place is equal to it in value, so that the Temple treasury is not defrauded.
gershom:b13.1: That “in place of” is an expression of associating: it implies [the transfer of sanctity] in substitution.
rashi:b8.2: Consecrated items of Temple maintenance: if he set a non-sacred animal [beside it] and said “this is the substitute of this,” or “the exchange for this.”
rashi:b8.3: He has not said anything: for it is an expression of substitution, and they do not effect substitution, as we said in the first chapter (above, 13a): consecrated items of Temple maintenance are excluded, etc.
rashi:b9.1:
“This is in place of this,” “this is desacralized onto this,” his statement stands: the consecrated item goes out to non-sacred status and this one enters in its place, for consecrated items of Temple maintenance can be redeemed even when unblemished. Evidently “in place of” is an expression of desacralization.
A version from the Land of Israel [lashon Yerushalmi]: Do their redemptions take hold? That is to say, do they effect substitution?
gershom:b14.1: [And the Gemara raises a contradiction: with consecrated items of Temple maintenance, if he said “the substitute of this” or “the exchange for this,” which is an expression of associating in substitution, he has said nothing, since consecrated items of Temple maintenance do not effect substitution. But if he said “this in place of this” or “this is desacralized onto this,” his statement stands, since that is not an expression of substitution but an expression of desacralization: let this go out and that enter. And if it enters your mind that “in place of” is an expression of associating in substitution…]
gershom:b16.1: Another version: consecrated items of Temple maintenance, do their redemptions take hold? That is to say, do their substitutes take hold?
gershom:b15.1: What is different in the first clause, [which says he has said nothing,] and what is different in the latter clause, which says his statement stands?
